headline: A violent AI-led selloff after the Democratic midterm sweep wiped out the Nasdaq's gains and hit Asia hardest, and futures are steadying ahead of today's jobs report. Healthcare policy and dealmaking continue underneath, with a reported $10 billion AstraZeneca bid for Rhythm the standout.
watch: October US jobs report and whether Thursday's tech-led rout extends or fades
Taiwan's stabilization fund and any further intervention in Asian equities
Rhythm Pharmaceuticals' response to the reported AstraZeneca approach
Anthropic IPO pricing talk and the effect on AI-related issuance
Oil near $100 and the direction of US-Iran mediation

paragraphs.text: The biggest deal story is a report from the Wall Street Journal, relayed by Fierce Biotech, that AstraZeneca has offered roughly $10 billion for Rhythm Pharmaceuticals, a rare obesity-disease company. At least three analyst teams think a bidding war is possible and doubt Rhythm will accept the current pitch. This is a reported approach, not an agreed deal, and nothing is confirmed from either company. Smaller M&A also moved. ANI Pharmaceuticals will pay $560 million for Sweden's Egetis Therapeutics and its approved orphan drug Emcitate, Dipharma is buying the UK rare disease partner LogixX Pharma, and Ellipsis Health bought Kouper Health to expand AI voice calling for patients. Rare disease assets keep drawing strategic buyers.

paragraphs.text: Private funding was active. T-Therapeutics raised a $133 million Series B for T cell receptor bispecifics, with Johnson & Johnson, Merck KGaA, Eli Lilly and Sanofi named as backers. Alethio, an Oxford spinout, took in $90 million for a rare blood cancer antibody, and Anaheim Bio launched with €40 million. Aulis Capital closed a $200 million debut fund for cross-border biotech, and Healthcare Today says biotech venture capital is heading for a record year. On the public side, Rezera, formerly NodThera, is targeting a $181 million IPO to fund a phase 3 NLRP3 program. Cloudbreak Pharma posted a phase 3 win while caught up in an IPO investigation, which echoes the regulatory halt on OPay's NYSE listing. China licensing continues, with Caldera and Evommune signing deals and Evommune paying $30 million upfront to Hinova in a roughly $1 billion molecular glue pact.

paragraphs.text: On the commercial side, Revolution Medicines reported $198 million of first-quarter Rasonque sales in about five weeks. Analysts called it eye-popping, though management cautioned against extrapolating. Novartis confirmed nine Zolgensma patients have developed tumors, seven of them newly disclosed, and the causal link is not established in what we can see. Alnylam is searching for a new chief commercial officer as Amvuttra's trajectory falters, and Agios is cutting more than 100 R&D roles ahead of a hoped-for sickle cell approval. Elsewhere, Merck shared mid-stage MASH biopsy data on the Hanmi-licensed dual agonist, and J&J and AbbVie are set to show early trispecific myeloma data at ASH. Vanda drew an FDA rebuke over a Nereus TV ad. European healthcare stocks fell with the wider market, which Wealth Club linked possibly to profit-taking.

paragraphs.text: Policy news leans negative for providers. CMS finalized 2027 rules that cut Medicare physician pay and trim 340B drug payments while expanding site-neutral payments. Hospitals and doctors objected, and Fierce Healthcare says the outpatient rule moderated some of the proposed shifts but left them largely intact. Reports differ on remote patient monitoring: STAT says the vendor ban was pushed to 2029, while Fierce says CMS is moving ahead with restrictions, so details are worth checking. The administration is also cutting off two No Surprises Act arbitration groups, one of which let doctors win 96 percent of disputes. A court blocked CMS's moratorium on new ACA broker registrations. On science, Democrats now in control of Congress are preparing to push back on the administration's research overhaul.

paragraphs.text: Insurers had a good quarter. Cigna raised its 2026 outlook on insurance and specialty pharmacy profits, though Express Scripts is a drag. Third-quarter profit was $1.44 billion, below last year's $1.87 billion. Oscar called it its strongest year, with membership up 27% to 2.7 million. Clover lifted its outlook on $130 million of profit, and hospital operator Ardent raised guidance on volume and lower labor spend. Separately, the Journal reports that CVS is planning to split its drugstore and insurance businesses after a secret strategic review, and Elevance sued autism-therapy provider the Perfect Child over $160 million in alleged overpayments. Public health items include a first Wisconsin measles death since 1990 and a Washington State bird flu death.

paragraphs.text: Thursday was a rout. The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4% and Wall Street shed about $3.2 trillion, per the FT. The S&P 500 had its worst day since April 2025, the Nasdaq Composite entered correction territory, and the Dow lost more than 1,800 points. Bloomberg says trend-following systematic funds amplified the move into a record one-day value plunge in the Nasdaq 100. The trigger was investor doubt over the durability of AI spending, set off by the Democratic midterm sweep, which several outlets say upended AI-related trades. Calls for tougher limits on data centers from Democratic winners and Texas's governor-elect, who wants community approval first, add a political leg to the AI-infrastructure story.

paragraphs.text: The damage spread globally and was worst in Asia. Japan's Nikkei and Topix fell nearly 6% in their biggest one-day drop since the April tariff chaos, and the NYT says Japan's market entered a bear market. Taiwan's benchmark had its worst week in 25 years, and authorities there activated the National Financial Stabilization Fund, following South Korea. India and Europe were relative bright spots, according to Bloomberg. Futures are rebounding, with dip buyers appearing and the FT expecting small gains at the open. The FT notes the selloff is deep but not yet broad. CNBC flags rotation out of tech as a risk to the wider market, even as homebuilders, consumer discretionary names and solar stocks have benefited from the election result.

paragraphs.text: Today's US jobs report is the main data point. Initial claims fell to 189,000, below the 197,000 expected. The Fed held rates last week, per the NYT, and is widely expected to hike gradually in December. Williams said it is the right time to gather more data before settling on the policy stance, and Barkin foresees gradual hikes. Treasury yields turned higher before the data, and the Journal argues bonds look compelling after the equity selloff. The dollar index reached a one-week high, with ING expecting it to trade in a 101.500 to 102.500 range.

paragraphs.text: Abroad, the Bank of England raised its rate to 4%, its first increase in three years, with Governor Bailey signalling more to come on fears of entrenched inflation. Norway held but signalled readiness to tighten, and Malaysia held. Thailand's inflation overshot its target on fuel costs. Eurozone retail sales fell as energy prices weighed on confidence, though German industrial production rose unexpectedly in September. Oil slid below $100 a barrel on hopes the war with Iran might wind down, and the FT reports Qatar-led mediators pushing for an interim deal. Ukraine's strikes on a sixth Russian refinery in a week pull the other way. UN data show global food prices eased in October.

paragraphs.text: Earnings were mixed. DraftKings cut guidance while spending on a prediction-market push against Kalshi and Polymarket. Tesla will wind down Cybertruck output in Texas as Musk pivots to robotics and AI. IAG cut capacity and investment plans and warned of higher fares in 2027 as it has less fuel hedging. Daimler Truck confirmed guidance on 12% order growth in North America. Cloudflare jumped on its fastest sales growth in nearly four years, and Iren rebounded on a new cloud deal. The Hong Kong exchange operator's profit unexpectedly slipped as trading cooled. The WSJ also warns profits may be near their peak.

paragraphs.text: The sharpest warning on private credit comes from Benzinga, which quotes experts saying the surge in payment-in-kind interest is pushing problems down the road. We only have the headline framing, with no figures, so the scale is unclear. PIK lets borrowers pay interest in additional debt instead of cash, which can hide stress until refinancing or maturity. After a sharp equity selloff, with AI-linked borrowers and the data-center financings behind them under scrutiny, that distinction matters more. Wells Fargo's corporate and investment banking head also discussed the bank's approach to AI infrastructure financing, and Iren said its backlog is largely tied to investment-grade counterparties.

paragraphs.text: Fundraising and product launches show managers still pushing into wealth channels. Clearlake is tapping private wealth with a new platform, Partners Group broadened its private-credit platform with a new strategy, and Ark Invest wants to offer tokenised, exchange-traded interval funds with venture capital exposure. Blackstone is doubling lock-up periods for some Asian investors in BXPE, with withdrawals in the first four years penalised for clients in Singapore and Hong Kong. That is a reminder that liquidity terms are being tightened even as distribution widens. Goldman Sachs Asset Management published an LP survey on alternatives, but only the title is visible.

paragraphs.text: Direct lending and specialty finance continue. Victory Park backed construction lender Billd with a $100 million facility, and Northern Arc's diversified debt fund reached a first close of over ₹400 crore. In high yield, Rhône Group's MAXAM completed a €175 million tap, advised by Linklaters. For fixed-income investors, Morningstar looks at a PIMCO bond ETF that has gone active, and the Journal argues Treasury yields are attractive. Among banks, the Fed terminated an enforcement action against Allegiant United Holdings, Nano Financial Holdings and Nano Banc. Retail savings rates of up to 5.00% are still being advertised, which sets a high bar for cash alternatives.

paragraphs.text: The equity-market rout hit the pipeline of AI-linked issuance. The Telegraph says Anthropic's IPO is in turmoil as the selloff hammers its valuation, Newser says investors doubt it can pull off a $100 billion listing, and TokenPost reports valuation pushback. FT Alphaville also commented on the IPO. These are early reports with limited detail, and nothing on terms or timing is confirmed in what we can see. Separately, regulators halted OPay's NYSE IPO with an inquiry. Rezera is still pursuing its $181 million biotech IPO, and Cloudbreak is under investigation in the same IPO wave.

paragraphs.text: In public M&A, Wendy's board rejected an offer from Nelson Peltz's hedge fund, and Monte dei Paschi raised profit guidance while weighing a takeover offer from Intesa Sanpaolo. The FT says China blocked SoftBank's acquisition of a robotics business, though few details were given. Wells Fargo's Fernando Rivas describes a now-or-never attitude to M&A, with clients rushing to act before incoming Democratic majorities. Debevoise is looking to year-end deals to stop its M&A ranking slide, and the FT says Macquarie's outgoing chief sees runway for growth after half-year profit rose 50% to A$2.5 billion. In regional banking, two Indiana banks agreed a $33 million merger, expected to close in the first half of 2027.
